Beaumont-Hamel British Cemetery is a Commonwealth War Graves Commission cemetery located near the village of Beaumont-Hamel in northern France. Some key facts about this cemetery:

- It contains the graves of over 2,300 soldiers who died during the Battle of the Somme in World War I. The majority of those buried there were British and Newfoundland troops.

- The cemetery was established in 1920 to consolidate smaller battlefield graves in the surrounding area. It was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens, a prominent British architect.

- The cemetery has two main sections - one for identified burials and one for unidentified burials. Many of the identified burials are of soldiers from the Newfoundland Regiment, who suffered devastating casualties during the first day of the Battle of the Somme on July 1, 1916.

- A distinctive feature of the cemetery is the Cross of Sacrifice, a tall stone cross erected to commemorate the fallen. There is also a Stone of Remembrance, as is typical in Commonwealth war cemeteries.

- The cemetery is located near the Newfoundland Memorial Park, which includes the preserved Beaumont-Hamel Newfoundland Memorial that marks the site of the Newfoundland Regiment's attack on July 1, 1916.

- Beaumont-Hamel British Cemetery is now maintained by the Commonwealth War Graves Commission as an important site for remembering those who died in one of the bloodiest battles of World War I on the Western Front.
